{{Short description|Swedish neuroethologist}}

[[File:Hansson Bill 8977.jpg | thumb | 220x124px | right | alt= Bill Hansson |
Bill Hansson]]
'''Bill S. Hansson''' (born 1959) is a Swedish [[neuroethologist]]. From June 2014 until June 2020, he was vice president of the [[Max Planck Society]].<ref>[http://www.mpg.de/8253783/Team-Stratmann ''The team around Martin Stratmann''] MPG Info, June 5, 2014</ref>

== Scientific career ==
Hansson studied biology at [[Lund University]] where he received a Bachelor of Science degree in biology in 1982. In 1988 he defended his PhD thesis in [[Ecology]]. From 1989 to 1990 he worked as postdoc at the [[University of Arizona]] and returned 1990 to a junior professorship in Lund. In 1992 he became Associate Professor and from 2000 until 2001 he was a Professor for [[Chemical ecology|Chemical Ecology]] at Lund University (2000). From 2001 he was Professor and Head of the Chemical Ecology department at the [[Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences]] (SLU) in [[Alnarp]], [[Sweden]]. He also served as vice dean for the Faculty of Landscape Planning, Horticulture, and Agriculture from 2003, until he was appointed Director and Scientific Member at the [[Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology]] in [[Jena]], Germany in 2006. He was head of the Department of Evolutionary [[Neuroethology]].<ref name="Webpage of the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology">[http://www.ice.mpg.de MPI for Chemical Ecology Website]</ref> until his retirement in 2025. Between 2014 and 2020 Hansson also served as Vice President of the [[Max Planck Society]]. He is now emeritus Director at the Jena institute. In 2025 he took up the position as Distinguished Professor at the Agricultural Genomics Institute in [[Shenzhen]], [[Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences]]. He also holds positions as Honorary Professor at the [[University of Jena]], at the [[Nanjing Agricultural University]] and at [[Hainan University]], and as emeritus Professor at SLU.

Hansson's research focuses on neuroethological aspects of insect-insect and insect-plant interactions. He is mainly studying [[insect olfaction]],<ref>[http://www.mpg.de/797216/F002_Focus_024-031.pdf ''Olfactory Research Is a Precision Business''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180712020636/https://www.mpg.de/797216/F002_Focus_024-031.pdf |date=2018-07-12 }} MaxPlanckResearch Magazine 3 /2009</ref> where his central questions are: How is semiochemical information (odors) detected by the antenna and processed in the [[insect brain]], how did these detection and processing systems evolve, and how does olfaction guide insect [[behavior]]?<ref>[http://www.mpg.de/1373937/moth_antennae ''Molecular messages from the antennae''] MPG News, April 15, 2011</ref><ref>[https://www.npr.org/blogs/thesalt/2012/12/06/166656957/fruitfly-nose-says-steer-clear-of-deadly-food-human-nose-not-so-reliable ''Fruit Fly Nose Says Steer Clear Of Deadly Food''] National Public Radio USA, Dec. 6, 2012</ref> He also compares these systems to other land-living [[arthropods]], as the [[giant robber crab]] on [[Christmas Island]].<ref>[http://news.sciencemag.org/sciencenow/2005/01/26-03.html?ref=hp ''A Nose for Survival''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130610022815/http://news.sciencemag.org/sciencenow/2005/01/26-03.html?ref=hp |date=2013-06-10 }} Science Now, Jan. 26, 2005</ref>
